docs.title: Fill-A-Bot Pump Control
docs.text: Clay Belsher | EGR 304

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: Fill-A-Bot is an automated water-dispensing system that fills a container to a selected amount. The main controller coordinates the user controls, measurement subsystems, and pump board to start dispensing and stop at the target. My responsibility is the pump-control subsystem, including its local power circuit, motor driver, and digital command connections.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My board uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano to receive two digital command signals from the main controller. CMD0 connects to RC3, CMD1 connects to RC2, and ribbon pin 8 provides a common ground. RA2 controls the motor-switching circuit.

The board includes a barrel-jack power input, fuse, 5V linear regulator, motor flyback protection, and a debug LED and button. The current single-MOSFET driver requires an H-bridge revision for forward-and-reverse operation. The linked design pages explain the component choices, configuration, calculations, and remaining decisions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
My subsystem controls the Fill-A-Bot water pump. The main control board sends two digital command signals through the ribbon connector: CMD0 connects to RC3, and CMD1 connects to RC2. Ribbon pin 8 provides a common ground between boards.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano reads these inputs and controls the MOSFET through RA2. The MOSFET switches the pump’s connection to ground. The gate resistor limits current during switching, and the pull-down resistor keeps the MOSFET off when the control output is not driving it. The 1N5822 flyback diode provides a path for motor current when the MOSFET switches off, limiting the voltage spike.

The barrel jack supplies power locally. The L7805 provides a 5V supply for the control electronics, while the pump uses the motor supply directly. Power is not supplied through the ribbon connector.

docs.title: Design Decisions
docs.text:
The main controller sends a two-bit pump command, written as C1 C0. Ribbon pin 1 carries C1 to RC3, and ribbon pin 2 carries C0 to RC2. The commands are 00 = Stop, 01 = Run, 10 = Stop, and 11 = Stop. The pump runs only while the command is 01. Ribbon pin 8 provides common ground.

The motor uses a separate power path because it requires more current than a microcontroller pin can supply. All control and motor grounds share a common reference.

docs.title: Remaining Design Work
docs.text:
The current single-MOSFET circuit supports one-direction operation. An H-bridge is still needed to meet the forward-and-reverse requirement.

The diagram currently shows a 12V supply. This must be reconciled with the project’s specified 9V adapter before the power design is finalized. Motor current, regulator heating, and the Curiosity Nano external-power configuration also need verification.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text: Fill-A-Bot — Pump Control Subsystem

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
My subsystem controls the 12V water pump used to move water from the reservoir into the container. The main controller sends two digital command signals to my PIC18F57Q43, which determines how the motor should operate.

I selected the components based on motor control, power requirements, ease of assembly, and compatibility with the other boards. The design now uses a DRV8871 H-bridge instead of the original single-MOSFET circuit because the motor needs to operate in both directions.

The schematic and block diagram reflect the 12V design. The final supply arrangement and motor performance still need to be confirmed during testing.

docs.title: Water Pump and Motor
docs.text:
The pump needs to provide a useful flow rate while allowing the system to stop dispensing consistently. I also wanted a pump that could be mounted outside the reservoir and connected using tubing.

Option Estimated Cost Advantages Limitations Gikfun R385 $10.88 External mounting, compact design, useful advertised flow rate Startup current and reverse operation need testing Adafruit 1150 Peristaltic Pump $24.95 Water stays inside tubing, easier cleaning Higher cost and slower flow DFRobot FIT0200 $9.20 Compact and inexpensive Submersible design makes maintenance less convenient

Selected component: Gikfun R385 12V Water Pump

I selected the R385 because it fits our planned tubing arrangement and provides a reasonable balance between size, flow rate, and cost.

The pump assembly includes the DC motor, so a separate motor purchase is not required.

Reversing the motor electrically does not guarantee that the pump will move water backward. I will verify its actual behavior when the hardware is available.

docs.title: Motor Driver
docs.text:
The motor cannot be powered directly from the PIC because its current requirements exceed what a microcontroller output can provide.

My original design used a MOSFET to switch the pump on and off. That approach worked for single-direction operation but did not meet the forward-and-reverse requirement.

Option Advantages Limitations AOTF2618L MOSFET Simple circuit, suitable for basic switching Cannot reverse the motor by itself Discrete H-bridge Supports forward and reverse operation Requires more components and design work TI DRV8871 H-bridge Integrated bidirectional motor driver with current regulation Current limit and thermal performance must be verified

Selected component: Texas Instruments DRV8871

I selected the DRV8871 because it provides bidirectional motor control in one integrated device. The PIC supplies the control signals, while the driver handles the motor current.

The DRV8871 uses two control inputs and two motor outputs. This allows the subsystem to control motor direction without sending motor current through the PIC.

The design includes a 68kΩ resistor connected to the driver's ILIM input.

Using the datasheet equation:

I_TRIP = 64 / R_ILIM(kΩ)

I_TRIP = 64 / 68 ≈ 0.94A

This provides an estimated nominal current-trip threshold of 0.94A. I will check whether that setting is appropriate after measuring the pump's operating and startup current.

The DRV8871 handles inductive motor-current recirculation through its internal switching circuitry. The separate flyback diode from my original MOSFET design is no longer used across the motor.

DRV8871 Datasheet

docs.title: Microcontroller
docs.text:
Selected component: Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano

I already have the Curiosity Nano from previous lab work, and it provides the digital inputs and outputs needed for this subsystem.

The PIC receives commands from the main controller, interprets the requested operating state, and sends control signals to the DRV8871.

The command structure is:

Command Operation 00 Stop 01 Forward 10 Reserved / Stop 11 Reverse

These are the commands interpreted by the PIC, not the DRV8871's direct input truth table.

Using direct digital signals also meets our team's requirement for pin-to-pin communication without UART or I2C.

docs.title: Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
The control electronics require a regulated 5V supply. I compared three linear regulators before selecting the L7805.

Option Estimated Cost Advantages Limitations ST L7805CV $1.08 Fixed 5V output, simple implementation Heat dissipation at higher input voltages TI LM2940CT-5.0 $2.00 Lower dropout voltage More expensive and requires specific output capacitor characteristics ST LM317T $1.13 Adjustable output Requires additional resistors to set 5V

Selected component: ST L7805CV

I selected the L7805 because it provides a fixed 5V output without requiring an adjustable resistor network.

The regulator supplies the control electronics, not the pump motor. Input and output capacitors help maintain stable operation.

Since the design uses a nominal 12V input, I will check regulator heating during testing. I also need to verify the correct external-power configuration for the Curiosity Nano before connecting the regulated supply.

L7805 Datasheet

docs.title: Power Supply and Protection
docs.text:
The current schematic uses a nominal 12V supply for the pump driver and the input of the 5V regulator.

Supply Option Estimated Cost Output Consideration MEAN WELL GST25A12-P1J $18.32 12V, 2.08A Lowest-cost option in the original comparison MEAN WELL GST40A12-P1J $22.93 12V, 3.34A Additional current capacity MEAN WELL GST60A12-P1J $24.86 12V, 5A More capacity than currently estimated

Current design voltage: 12V

The R385 pump kit was selected for the 12V design. The final supply must still be checked against the course requirements and measured motor current.

Each subsystem has its own barrel-jack power connection. The ribbon cable is used for communication and a shared ground reference, not to distribute motor power.

The schematic also includes a fuse for input overcurrent protection. Fuse suitability, supply polarity, and connector ratings need to be checked before hardware testing.

docs.title: Communication and Connections
docs.text:
The main controller communicates with my subsystem through an eight-pin ribbon connector.

The team interface reserves five positions for digital signals, two for analog signals, and one for ground. My subsystem currently uses two digital command signals and the common ground connection.

Connection Function CMD0 and CMD1 Digital commands received by the PIC Common GND Shared signal reference between boards PIC motor-control outputs Control the DRV8871 inputs DRV8871 motor outputs Connect to the two terminals of the R385 pump motor 12V supply Powers the motor driver 5V regulator output Supplies the control electronics

I chose direct pin-to-pin communication because it keeps the interface straightforward and avoids requiring a separate serial communication protocol.

The exact GPIO assignments for both H-bridge control inputs must match the latest KiCad schematic and firmware configuration.

docs.title: Supporting Components
docs.text:
Component Purpose DC barrel jack Independent power input Fuse Input overcurrent protection 68kΩ ILIM resistor Sets the DRV8871 current-trip threshold 0.1µF bypass capacitor Local high-frequency supply decoupling 47µF bulk capacitor Helps support changes in motor supply current Debug LED Visual indication during testing Debug pushbutton Manual test input Spare GPIO header Additional connections for testing Ribbon connector Communication with the other boards Pump connector Connection to the external 12V pump motor

Common resistors and capacitors are available through the lab. The PIC is already owned, so these items do not need to be purchased again.

docs.title: Firmware and MCC Configuration
docs.text:
I previously configured the PIC18F57Q43 using MCC Melody and generated initialization files for the original motor-control design.

The existing configuration includes the command inputs and local debugging connections. However, the firmware must be updated to drive both DRV8871 control inputs and interpret the reverse command correctly.

Download the MPLAB X project and MCC configuration

Generating the initialization files does not verify that the completed firmware operates the motor. That will require compilation and hardware testing.

docs.title: Testing and Verification
docs.text:
Once the hardware is assembled, I will verify the following:

  • The 12V input and regulated 5V supply operate correctly.
  • The PIC receives and interprets the command signals.
  • The DRV8871 responds correctly to forward, reverse, and stop commands.
  • The pump's operating and startup currents are compatible with the driver and current-limit setting.
  • The regulator and motor driver remain within acceptable temperatures.
  • The pump stops consistently and its behavior during reverse operation is understood.
  • The ribbon interface and shared ground work correctly with the other boards.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The main component choices are now established: the PIC18F57Q43 handles control logic, the DRV8871 drives the motor, the R385 pump moves water, and the L7805 provides the regulated control supply.

The design has progressed from a basic MOSFET switching circuit to a bidirectional motor-control subsystem. The next step is verifying the electrical connections and actual hardware performance before completing the PCB layout.

docs.title: Microcontroller
docs.text:
I'm using the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano for the control logic. It receives signals from the other boards and sends the motor-control signals to the H-bridge.

I already have the PIC, so it does not need to be ordered.

docs.title: Motor Driver
docs.text:
The DRV8871 H-bridge controls the pump motor. It allows the motor to run in either direction, which is needed for the forward and reverse operation.

Three DRV8871DDAR chips are included in the DigiKey request for the PCB and spares.

DRV8871 Motor Driver - DigiKey

The current-limit resistor is R1, which is 68k ohms.

The nominal current-trip calculation is:

I_TRIP = 64 / 68 = 0.94 A

This value will be checked once the pump is available for testing.

docs.title: Breadboard Testing
docs.text:
The DRV8871DDAR is a surface-mount component, so it cannot plug directly into a breadboard.

One Adafruit DRV8871 breakout board is included in the DigiKey order to make testing easier before assembling the PCB.

The breakout board will be used to test the pump and motor-control signals. Header pins will need to be soldered before using it on a breadboard.

docs.title: Fuse Protection
docs.text:
The board uses a 1A slow-blow fuse on the power input.

Three Littelfuse 0218001.MXP fuses and two fuse holders are included in the DigiKey request.

1A Slow-Blow Fuse - DigiKey

The fuse rating will be checked against the pump's actual current during testing.

docs.title: Power Supply
docs.text:
The pump-control subsystem is designed around a 12V DC supply.

The L7805 voltage regulator provides 5V for the control circuitry. The pump kit includes a 12V adapter, so a separate power adapter is not being ordered.

docs.title: Pump
docs.text:
The selected pump is the Gikfun EK1912 R385 12V diaphragm water pump kit.

The kit includes the pump, power adapter, and tubing needed for initial testing.

docs.text:
The subsystem uses an eight-pin ribbon connector for communication with the other Fill-A-Bot boards.

The planned connections are:

  • Pins 1-5: Digital signals
  • Pins 6-7: Analog signals
  • Pin 8: Common ground

Each board has its own power input. The boards communicate through direct pin-to-pin signals rather than I2C or UART.

The planned motor-control commands are:

  • 00 = Stop
  • 01 = Forward
  • 11 = Reverse

docs.title: Schematic
docs.text: tags: - Fill-A-Bot - Pump Control - EGR304

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
My part of the Fill-A-Bot project focuses on controlling the water pump. The circuit uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano to receive commands from the main controller and a DRV8871 H-bridge to control the pump motor.

I designed the subsystem around three main requirements: reliable motor control, independent power distribution, and straightforward communication with the other boards. The schematic brings these functions together while keeping the higher-current motor circuit separate from the microcontroller's control signals.

docs.title: Schematic
docs.text:
View Full-Resolution Schematic PDF

Download KiCad Project ZIP

docs.title: Power Input and Protection
docs.text:
The board has its own DC barrel jack so it can receive power independently of the other subsystems. A 1A slow-blow fuse is included to protect the input against excessive current.

The design uses a nominal 12V supply for the pump motor. This allows the motor to receive power through the H-bridge without drawing its operating current through the microcontroller.

docs.title: Voltage Regulation
docs.text:
I selected the L7805 regulator to provide a 5V rail for the control electronics. The input and output capacitors help maintain stable operation when the supply experiences changes in load.

Since the regulator steps 12V down to 5V, heat dissipation is something I'll need to check during testing. I'll also verify the correct external-power configuration for the Curiosity Nano.

docs.title: Microcontroller
docs.text:
The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano handles the control logic for the subsystem. It reads the incoming digital commands and determines whether the pump should stop, run forward, or run in reverse.

Using the PIC for command processing also gives me flexibility to adjust the motor-control behavior in firmware without changing the communication method between boards.

docs.title: Motor Driver
docs.text:
I selected the DRV8871 H-bridge because the pump-control subsystem needs to support both forward and reverse motor operation. A single MOSFET can switch the motor on and off, but it cannot reverse the motor's polarity on its own.

The DRV8871 handles the motor current while the PIC provides the logic signals. This keeps the high-current switching separate from the microcontroller's GPIO pins.

The driver uses a 68kΩ current-limit resistor. Based on the DRV8871 current-limit equation:

I_TRIP = 64 / 68 ≈ 0.94A

This gives a nominal current-trip threshold of approximately 0.94A. I'll confirm that this setting is appropriate once the pump's actual operating and startup currents have been measured.

DRV8871 Datasheet

docs.title: Motor Control Logic
docs.text:
The subsystem receives two digital command signals from the main controller. I chose a simple two-bit command structure because it provides the required operating states without needing a more complicated communication protocol.

Command Operation 00 Stop 01 Forward 10 Reserved / Stop 11 Reverse

The PIC interprets these commands and sets the DRV8871 inputs accordingly. These are the subsystem commands, not the driver's direct input truth table.

docs.title: Team Communication
docs.text:
The board communicates with the main controller through an eight-pin ribbon connector. Following the class interface requirements, the connector reserves five pins for digital signals, two for analog signals, and one for ground.

Ribbon Pin Function 1–5 Digital signals 6–7 Analog signals 8 Shared ground

Communication is handled through direct pin-to-pin connections rather than UART or I2C. This keeps the interface simple and allows the boards to exchange logic signals without additional communication hardware.

Each subsystem also has its own power input, so the ribbon connector is used for communication and a common ground reference rather than distributing power between boards.

docs.title: Debugging and Testing
docs.text:
I included a debug LED, pushbutton, and spare GPIO connections to make troubleshooting easier as the hardware is assembled.

Once the components arrive, I'll start by checking the power rails and confirming that the PIC responds correctly to the incoming commands. From there, I'll test the H-bridge with the pump and measure its current during normal operation and startup.

I'll also check regulator heating, motor stopping behavior, and whether reversing the motor produces the intended fluid movement. These tests will help determine whether any changes are needed before the final PCB design.

docs.text: Clay Belsher — Fill-A-Bot Pump Control

docs.title: Preliminary Design Estimate
docs.text:
This budget uses the course spreadsheet template for my pump board. I have the Curiosity Nano and basic lab components, but I do not have the pump yet. The current values are planning assumptions, not measurements or verified maximum ratings.

The calculation uses a 9V input to match the project requirement. My current schematic still shows 12V and needs to be updated after the supply and pump choices are resolved.

Load Assumed current Basis Proposed R385 pump 500mA Placeholder for operating-load planning; startup and stall current unknown. Complete Curiosity Nano 100mA Whole-board planning allowance, not a datasheet maximum or measured value. External debug LED 5mA Upper-bound allowance using the 5V rail and 1kΩ series resistor. Other control loads 1mA Allowance for pull-ups and gate drive; switching configuration still needs verification. L7805 own operating current 10mA Planning allowance, not a verified maximum.

docs.title: Results Under These Assumptions
docs.text:
Result Calculated value 5V control load 106mA 5V load with 25% margin 132.5mA Regulator input current, including own operating current 116mA Total adapter operating current 616mA Adapter current with 25% margin 770mA Adapter operating input power at 9V 5.544W Regulator heat at 9V, including assumed own current 0.514W Regulator heat at original 12V assumption 0.862W

The pump receives motor-supply power directly. Its current does not pass through the 5V regulator. The source total includes the regulator input current once; it does not add the 5V load again.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
These assumptions give a preliminary source requirement of 770mA after a 25% margin. That number does not establish that an adapter will start the motor or handle a stall. The adapter model and current rating remain unselected.

The budget must be revised using the actual pump current and the final H-bridge design. H-bridge losses and control demand are not included yet. Regulator temperature and the Nano external-power configuration also need verification. The regulator heat estimates do not establish that a heat sink is unnecessary.

No battery or separate 3.3V rail is used. Other team boards are outside this individual budget, and the ribbon connector does not supply their power.
